LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Forgive, Accept, Respect & Include — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson is the deeper course of friendship: four words for the wobbles and the differences that every real group of children eventually meets.

What is this?

Forgive starts the game again after a fight, accept lets people be different without losing friendship, respect treats every person as valuable, and include opens the circle so nobody stands outside it.

What does it mean?

These four words make groups kind — a playdate of two only needs sorry and share, but a classroom of twenty runs on forgive, accept, respect and include. They are the civilisation words of childhood.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: forgive means the fight does not follow you into the next game; accept means different is allowed (different foods, different families, different speeds); and respect is NOT hitting, NOT mocking, and DO listening — even when you disagree.

Why this matters

The earlier friendship card taught the ladder (smile, care, forgive, friend); this one deepens it for real groups — the messy, wonderful, many-person world of preschool, where differences and conflicts arrive together.

What it teaches

Conflict recovery at group scale, acceptance of difference (the root of inclusion later), respect as behaviour (not feeling), and circle-keeping — the social architecture of making room.

Words to learn

forgiveacceptrespectincludedifferentcirclefresh start

Say this to your child

“"Friendship in a big group needs four strong words. Forgive — when someone messes up, we start fresh; the fight does not follow us to the next game. Accept — people are different, and different is allowed: different snacks, different homes, different speeds. Respect — I treat you like you matter: I do not hit, I do not mock, I DO listen. And include — the circle opens; there is always room for one more. Those are the words that make a group kind. Any group. Even this family."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four deeper friendship words."
  2. Read the panels: clasped hands FORGIVE, the open-armed girl ACCEPTS, the thoughtful boy RESPECTS, the welcoming girl INCLUDES.
  3. Play the open-circle game below — the circle literally opens wider every time someone is let in.
  4. Sort the differences: "some friends eat different food, some families have one parent, some kids talk later — is different okay?" (Always yes; different is the point.)
  5. Close with the takeaway: "forgive the past, accept the difference, respect the person, include the everyone."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels hold the deep friendship words: Forgive, a boy with clasped hands and calm eyes; Accept, a girl with her arms open wide; Respect, a thoughtful boy with a hand to his chin; and Include, a girl welcoming with open arms — the group values drawn at child scale.

Ask your child

"What does forgive do with yesterday’s fight?" "Is different okay?" "What does respect NOT do?" "What does include do with the circle?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Forgive means fresh start!" "Different is okay" or the observer: "we let him play even though he is little."

Out in the real world

Deep friendship moments recur all week: the sibling truce after the storm (forgive), the friend who eats different food (accept), the quiet kid who hates being teased (respect), the newcomer at music class (include). Each one is a rep — name the word where the moment lives.

Try it together

The Open-Circle Game: four or more toys (or people) form a tight circle playing a simple ball-pass. A fifth toy approaches — shy, outside. The circle’s job: make the circle BIGGER, not tighter — include the newcomer, teach the game, pass to them second. Play three rounds; by the last one, your child is running the welcoming without a script.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which word starts things fresh? Which word makes room for different? Which one opens the circle?" Forgive, accept, include — three answers and the deeper friendship words are at work.

Parent tips

Respect is best taught by what it refuses to do — "in this family we do not mock, even when it is funny" — and what it always does: listen to the other side first. And separate forgive from consequences: "I forgive you, AND the rule still stands" is a sentence children need to hear; forgiveness is not amnesia.

This lesson pairs with the Forgive, Accept, Respect & Include flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
